claim: During slow-wave sleep, we are unresponsive but continue monitoring external events for survival.
source: We are unresponsive during slow-wave sleep but continue monitoring external events for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about slow-wave sleep that draws on established scientific understanding and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The brain wakens us when danger is imminent during sleep.
source: Our brain wakens us when danger is imminent.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about sleep protective mechanisms.

claim: Novel vocabulary consisting of simultaneously played pseudowords and translation words can be encoded/stored during sleep.
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined whether novel vocabulary consisting of simultaneously played pseudowords and translation words are encoded/stored during sleep, and which neural-electrical events facilitate encoding/storage.
evidence: This is the research question being tested in the study.

claim: Sleep-played vocabulary influenced awake decision-making 36 hr later when targeted to troughs.
source: The sleep-played vocabulary influenced awake decision-making 36 hr later, if targeted to troughs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Linguistic processing of words during sleep raised neural complexity.
source: The words' linguistic processing raised neural complexity.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental measurements of neural complexity.

claim: Semantic-associative encoding was supported by increased theta power during the ensuing peak.
source: The words' semantic-associative encoding was supported by increased theta power during the ensuing peak.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's EEG data analysis.

claim: Fast-spindle power ramped up during a second peak likely aiding consolidation.
source: Fast-spindle power ramped up during a second peak likely aiding consolidation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with an interpretive component about consolidation.

claim: New vocabulary played during slow-wave sleep was stored and influenced decision-making days later.
source: Hence, new vocabulary played during slow-wave sleep was stored and influenced decision-making days later.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The thalamic gating hypothesis claimed a blockade of sensory information at the thalamic level.
source: Although the thalamic gating hypothesis had claimed a blockade of sensory information at the thalamic level (McCormick and Bal, 1994), we now know that sleepers still monitor the environment for their safety and survival (Ai et al., 2018; Andrillon et al., 2016; Andrillon et al., 2017; Arzi et al., 2012; Blume et al., 2017; Koroma et al., 2022; Ruch et al., 2014; Ruch and Henke, 2020; Züst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCormick and Bal, 1994.

claim: Sleepers still monitor the environment for their safety and survival.
source: Although the thalamic gating hypothesis had claimed a blockade of sensory information at the thalamic level (McCormick and Bal, 1994), we now know that sleepers still monitor the environment for their safety and survival (Ai et al., 2018; Andrillon et al., 2016; Andrillon et al., 2017; Arzi et al., 2012; Blume et al., 2017; Koroma et al., 2022; Ruch et al., 2014; Ruch and Henke, 2020; Züst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: The sleeping brain decides whether an external event can be disregarded, requires immediate awakening or should be stored for later consideration.
source: The sleeping brain decides whether an external event can be disregarded, requires immediate awakening or should be stored for later consideration in the waking state (Ameen et al., 2022; Blume et al., 2018; Formby, 1967; Holeckova et al., 2006; Moyne et al., 2022; Oswald et al., 1960; Türker et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Processing of external information during sleep versus wakefulness is reduced.
source: Although the processing of external information during sleep versus wakefulness is reduced (Andrillon et al., 2016), sleep still allows for the detection of semantic incongruity (Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999; Ibáñez et al., 2006) and the detection of rule violations (Ruby et al., 2008; Strauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andrillon et al., 2016.

claim: Sleep allows for the detection of semantic incongruity.
source: Although the processing of external information during sleep versus wakefulness is reduced (Andrillon et al., 2016), sleep still allows for the detection of semantic incongruity (Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999; Ibáñez et al., 2006) and the detection of rule violations (Ruby et al., 2008; Strauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999 and Ibáñez et al., 2006.

claim: Sleep allows for the detection of rule violations.
source: Although the processing of external information during sleep versus wakefulness is reduced (Andrillon et al., 2016), sleep still allows for the detection of semantic incongruity (Bastuji and García-Larrea, 1999; Ibáñez et al., 2006) and the detection of rule violations (Ruby et al., 2008; Strauss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ruby et al., 2008 and Strauss et al., 2015.

claim: The sleeping brain can store new information, ranging from tone-odor to word-word associations.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that the sleeping brain cannot only process information, but can store new information, ranging from tone-odor to word-word associations (Ai et al., 2018; Andrillon and Kouider, 2016; Arzi et al., 2012; Ataei et al., 2023; de Lavilléon et al., 2015; Koroma et al., 2022; Züst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: It remains unclear whether and under what circumstances episodic memory formation can proceed during deep sleep.
source: However, it remains unclear whether and under what circumstances the most sophisticated form of human learning, namely episodic memory formation, can proceed during deep sleep (Ruch and Henke, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Episodic memory refers to the recollection of personally experienced episodes.
source: The term episodic memory refers to the recollection of personally experienced episodes (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Tulving, 2002.

claim: Episodic memory formation depends on hippocampal-neocortical interactions.
source: Episodic memory formation depends on hippocampal-neocortical interactions (Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993; Henke, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen and Eichenbaum, 1993 and Henke, 2010.

claim: Episodic memory was long associated with wakefulness and conscious awareness of events.
source: Because episodic memory belongs to declarative/explicit memory, episodic memory was long associated with wakefulness and conscious awareness of events (Gabrieli, 1998; Moscovitch, 2008; Schacter, 1998; Squire and Dede, 2015; Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is a historical perspective supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hippocampal-assisted episodic memory formation may proceed without conscious awareness of the learning material.
source: In the meantime, counterevidence suggests that hippocampal-assisted episodic memory formation may also proceed without conscious awareness of the learning material (Duss et al., 2014; Reber et al., 2012; Schneider et al., 2021; Züst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: Unconscious hippocampus-assisted episodic encoding of subliminal (invisible) words was revealed.
source: When applying such tasks, unconscious hippocampus-assisted episodic encoding of subliminal (invisible) words was revealed (Duss et al., 2014; Reber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duss et al., 2014 and Reber et al., 2012.

claim: Episodic memory is defined based on rapid formation of new associations calling on the hippocampus' ability for one-shot relational binding, and flexible retrieval of these associations in novel contexts.
source: Thus, in the current study, we define episodic memory based on its key computational properties, which are the rapid formation of new associations calling on the hippocampus' ability for one-shot relational binding, and the flexible retrieval of these associations in novel contexts.
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the study, based on established computational properties.

claim: The hippocampus ramps up its encoding machinery at 300–500 ms after word onset in awake learning experiments.
source: Awake learning experiments in humans indicated that the hippocampus ramps up its encoding machinery at 300–500 ms after word onset (Long et al., 2014; Quiroga et al., 2005; Staresina and Wimber, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Long et al., 2014, Quiroga et al., 2005, and Staresina and Wimber, 2019.

claim: Slow-wave sleep is characterized by an average neurochemical milieu and neural functional connectivity that does not favour episodic memory formation.
source: Although slow-wave sleep (deep sleep) is characterized by an average neurochemical milieu and neural functional connectivity that does not favour episodic memory formation, slow-wave sleep is not a unitary state.
evidence: This is a statement about the general characteristics of slow-wave sleep based on established knowledge.

claim: Slow-wave sleep is not a unitary state.
source: Although slow-wave sleep (deep sleep) is characterized by an average neurochemical milieu and neural functional connectivity that does not favour episodic memory formation, slow-wave sleep is not a unitary state.
evidence: This is a statement about the heterogeneity of slow-wave sleep.

claim: Neuronal activity and excitability waxes and wanes during slow-wave sleep, generating electroencephalographic slow-waves that oscillate at 1 Hz.
source: In fact, neuronal activity and excitability waxes and wanes during slow-wave sleep, thereby generating the eponymous electroencephalographic slow-waves that oscillate at 1 Hz and are characterised by slow-wave peaks and troughs.
evidence: This is a description of slow-wave characteristics based on established knowledge.

claim: A peak and a trough each last around 500 ms.
source: A peak and a trough each last around 500 ms (Berry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berry et al., 2015.

claim: Peaks of slow-waves are associated with high neural excitability and wake-like network characteristics.
source: Because peaks of slow-waves are associated with high neural excitability and wake-like network characteristics, peaks might provide the necessary plasticity mechanisms for episodic memory formation (Cox et al., 2014a; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2014a and Diba and Buzsáki, 2007.

claim: Züst et al., 2019 reported successful paired-associate learning in humans during peaks of slow-waves recorded in a mid-day nap.
source: Züst et al., 2019 reported successful paired-associate learning in humans during peaks of slow-waves recorded in a mid-day nap with the retrieval of the sleep-learned associations tested after awakening on the same day.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Peaks are the time windows when memories formed during previous days are replayed, strengthened, and consolidated.
source: Because peaks with their depolarized neural states are also the time windows when memories formed during the previous days are replayed, strengthened, and consolidated (Göldi et al., 2019; Mölle et al., 2002; Mölle et al., 2011; Muehlroth et al., 2019; Staresina et al., 2015), high-jacking peaks for de novo learning might impair ongoing memory consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Troughs are characterized by neural silence.
source: Troughs on the other hand are characterized by neural silence (Cox et al., 2014a; Destexhe et al., 2007; Schabus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2014a, Destexhe et al., 2007, and Schabus et al., 2012.

claim: The high background firing rate during the peak state favors synaptic down-scaling/depression rather than potentiation.
source: Furthermore, recent results suggest that the high background firing rate during the peak state favors synaptic down-scaling/depression rather than potentiation (Bartram et al., 2017; Yoshida and Toyoizumi, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bartram et al., 2017 and Yoshida and Toyoizumi, 2023.

claim: The trough rather than the peak state might be beneficial for de-novo memory formation during deep sleep.
source: Hence, the trough rather than the peak state might be beneficial for de-novo memory formation during deep sleep.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from previous findings.

claim: An average of 23.98 (SD 3.84) pairs of pseudowords and translation words were played to thirty healthy volunteers during their slow-wave night-sleep.
source: Thirty healthy male and female volunteers were acoustically stimulated during their slow-wave night-sleep with an average of 23.98 (SD 3.84) pairs of pseudowords and translation words.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and data.

claim: Word pairs were targeted either to slow-wave peaks or to troughs using a brain-state-dependent stimulation algorithm.
source: We targeted these word pairs either to slow-wave peaks or to troughs using our own slow wave phase-targeted, brain-state-dependent stimulation algorithm (TOPOSO, Ruch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Pseudowords and translation words were simultaneously played into the right ear and left ear, respectively.
source: Pseudowords and translation words were simultaneously played into the right ear and left ear, respectively (Aarons, 1990; Kimura, 1961).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with supporting citations.

claim: Word pairs' presentation lasted on average 540 ms (SEM = 0.011 ms).
source: Their presentation lasted on average 540 ms (SEM = 0.011 ms).
evidence: This is experimental data about stimulus duration.

claim: Word pairs' sound onset was ~100 ms before the local maxima of the targeted slow-wave phase.
source: Word pairs' sound onset was ~100 ms before the local maxima of the targeted slow-wave phase and largely fit into this half-wave (duration of slow-wave peaks/troughs: ~500 ms, duration of word pair presentation: 540 ms, overlap: 350 ms).
evidence: This is experimental data about the timing of stimulation.

claim: Each word pair was presented four times in succession to enhance the odds of their successful processing.
source: Each word pair was presented four times in succession to enhance the odds of their successful processing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: A mean of 95.33 (SD = 15.41) word pairs was played per participant.
source: Adding over the four repetitions, a mean of 95.33 (SD = 15.41) word pairs was played per participant.
evidence: This is experimental data about the number of stimuli presented.

claim: Over all conditions, associative retrieval performance exceeded chance performance by 2.67% (SD = 8.11), which just failed statistical significance.
source: Over all conditions, associative retrieval performance exceeded chance performance by 2.67% (SD = 8.11), which just failed statistical significance (F Intercept(1,28) = 3.490, p=0.077).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Retrieval performance over both encoding-test delays was significantly better when word pairs were targeted to Troughs rather than Peaks.
source: Retrieval performance over both encoding-test delays was significantly better when word pairs were targeted to Troughs rather than Peaks (main effect Peak versus Trough: F(1,28) = 5.237, p=0.030, d=0.865, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Retrieval performance did not differ significantly between the two encoding-test delays.
source: Retrieval performance did not differ significantly between the two encoding-test delays (main effect Encoding-Test Delay: F(1,28) = 0.571, p=0.456).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: There was no significant interaction between the factor Peak versus Trough and the factor Encoding-Test Delay.
source: There was no significant interaction between the factor Peak versus Trough and the factor Encoding-Test Delay (F(1,28) = 0.646, p=0.428).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Mean retrieval performance in the Trough condition was 5.77% above chance level.
source: This ANOVA established a significant intercept: mean retrieval performance was 5.77% above chance level (MTrough = 39.11%, SD = 10.76; FIntercept (1,14)=5.660, p=0.032).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Retrieval performance was numerically larger at 36 hours than at 12 hr in the Trough condition.
source: Although the 12 hr versus 36 hr comparison was not statistically significant (FEncoding-Test Delay (1,14)=1.308, p=0.272), retrieval performance was numerically larger at 36 hours than at 12 hr (M12hours=37.4%, SD = 9.0; M36hours=40.7%, SD = 12.4; Figure 2BC and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study shown in figures.

claim: Retrieval performance significantly exceeded chance at 36 hr only in the Trough condition.
source: Planned contrasts against chance level revealed that retrieval performance significantly exceeded chance at 36 hr only (P36hours=0.036, P12hours=0.094).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Participants consistently chose the same category for specific sleep-played pseudowords at the 12- and 36 hr retrieval test (12-to-36 hr consistency rate = 47%, chance level = 33.3%).
source: This item-based analysis revealed that participants consistently chose the same category (animals, tools, places) for specific sleep-played pseudowords at the 12- and 36 hr retrieval test (12-to-36 hr consistency rate = 47%, chance level = 33.3%).
evidence: This is a finding from the item-level analysis.

claim: The consistency rate did not differ significantly between the Trough and the Peak condition.
source: Moreover, the consistency rate did not differ significantly between the Trough and the Peak condition (MTrough = 47.2%, MPeak = 47.0%, p=0.98).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Participants in the Trough condition were more likely to assign pseudowords to the correct category at 36 hr when they were already correct at 12 hr.
source: Participants in the Trough condition were more likely to assign pseudowords to the correct category at 36 hr when they were already correct at 12 hr (Trough: 20% of all items at 36 hr, or 54% of all initially correctly assigned items; Peak: 14% of all items at 36 hr, or 42% of all initially correctly assigned items).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the item-level analysis.

claim: Participants in the Trough condition were more likely to switch assignments and use the correct category at 36 hr, if they had initially assigned them to an incorrect category at 12 hr.
source: Participants in the Trough condition were more likely to switch assignments and use the correct category at 36 hr, if they had initially assigned them to an incorrect category at 12 hr (Trough: 20% of all items at 36 hr, or 32% of the initially incorrectly assigned items; Peak: 18% of all items at 36 hr, or 27% of the initially incorrectly assigned items).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the item-level analysis.

claim: Word pairs were exclusively played during slow-wave sleep, which is accompanied by a loss of consciousness.
source: Because word pairs were exclusively played during slow-wave sleep, which is accompanied by a loss of consciousness (Dement and Kleitman, 1957; Massimini et al., 2012), encoding and retrieval must have been unconscious.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dement and Kleitman, 1957 and Massimini et al., 2012.

claim: Encoding and retrieval must have been unconscious.
source: Because word pairs were exclusively played during slow-wave sleep, which is accompanied by a loss of consciousness (Dement and Kleitman, 1957; Massimini et al., 2012), encoding and retrieval must have been unconscious.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that stimuli were presented during slow-wave sleep.

claim: Participants' feeling-of-having-heard (FoHH) responses in the Trough condition did not differ significantly between previously sleep-played pseudowords and new pseudowords.
source: Participants' feeling-of-having-heard (FoHH) responses in the Trough condition did not differ significantly between previously sleep-played pseudowords and new pseudowords that had not been played during sleep (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3; ANOVA factor 'sleep-played': F(1,14) = 0.45, p=0.51, Msleep-played_12hours=2.41, SD = 0.36, Mnew_12hours=2.42, SD = 0.353, Msleep-played_36hours=2.53, SD = 0.53, Mnew_36hours=2.56, SD = 0.618).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study shown in a figure supplement.

claim: There was no significant difference between the FoHH for correct versus incorrect category assignments.
source: We also found no significant difference between the FoHH for correct versus incorrect category assignments (ANOVA factor 'accuracy': F(1,14) = 0.09, p=0.77, M12hours_correct=2.37, SD = 0.54, M12hours_incorrect=2.42, SD = 0.39, M36hours_correct=2.57, SD = 0.62, M36hours_incorrect=2.49, SD = 0.55) and no difference between EC and CC trials (ANOVA factor "Association": F(1,14) = 0.09, p=0.77, M12hours_correct=2.37, SD = 0.54, M12hours_incorrect=2.42, SD = 0.39, M36hours_correct=2.57, SD = 0.62, M36hours_incorrect=2.49, SD = 0.55).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Participants could not consciously recognize sleep-played pseudowords.
source: These findings strongly suggest that participants could not consciously recognize sleep-played pseudowords.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FoHH data.

claim: Confidence ratings did not differ significantly for sleep-played compared to new pseudowords in the Trough condition.
source: Confidence ratings did not differ signifcantly for sleep-played (EC and CC) compared to new pseudowords in the Trough condition, were sleep-learning was successful ANOVA factor 'sleep-played': F(1,14) = 0.47, p=0.5; Msleep-played_12hours=2.17, SD = 0.38, Mnew_12hours=2.19, SD = 0.376, Msleep-played_36hours=2.26, SD = 0.426, Mnew_36hours=2.26, SD = 0.426.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Confidence ratings for correct versus incorrect category assignments in the experimental condition differed neither in the Trough condition nor the Peak condition.
source: Furthermore, confidence ratings for correct versus incorrect category assignments in the experimental condition differed neither in the Trough condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), ANOVA factor 'Accuracy': F(1,14) = 2.36, p=0.15; M12hours_correct=2.24, SD = 0.42, M12hours_incorrect=2.16, SD = 0.35, M36hours_correct=2.33, SD = 0.44, M36hours_incorrect=2.28, SD = 0.4 nor the Peak condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), ANOVA factor Accuracy: F(1,14) = 0.48, p=0.50; M12hours_correct=2.19, SD = 0.51, M12hours_incorrect=2.28, SD = 0.54, M36hours_correct=2.33, SD = 0.58, M36hours_incorrect=2.36, SD = 0.51.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study shown in a figure supplement.

claim: The word-evoked response in the Peak condition resembled the response to white noise clicks in slow-wave entrainment studies.
source: The word-evoked response in the Peak condition resembled the response to white noise clicks in slow-wave entrainment studies (Andrillon and Kouider, 2020; Cox et al., 2014b; Ngo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous research supported by citations.

claim: An early frontal positivity at 200 ms was followed by a large negative component at 550 ms, which in turn was followed by a late positivity at 900 ms in the Peak condition.
source: An early frontal positivity at 200 ms was followed by a large negative component at 550 ms, which in turn was followed by a late positivity at 900 ms (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the ERP components shown in Figure 3.

claim: These components have been described as the generic response of the sleeping brain to any kind of sensory stimulation.
source: These components have been described as the generic response of the sleeping brain to any kind of sensory stimulation (Andrillon and Kouider, 2020; Cox et al., 2014b; Laurino et al., 2014; Laurino et al., 2019; Riedner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: These components resemble K-complexes that reflect the brain's response to maintaining sleep in the presence of sensory stimuli.
source: Halász, 2016 suggested that these components resemble K-complexes that reflect the brain's response to maintaining sleep in the presence of sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Halász, 2016.

claim: When words were targeted to troughs, the played words evoked two positive frontal components.
source: However, when we targeted words to troughs, the played words evoked two positive frontal components.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: The first positive component appeared at 500 ms and the second at one second following word onset in the Trough condition.
source: The first positive component appeared at 500 ms and the second at one second following word onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: The ERP differences between the Trough and the Peak condition vanished at 700 ms.
source: The ERP differences between the Trough and the Peak condition vanished at 700 ms.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Between 700 ms and 2 s following word onset the EEG was comparable between the two conditions.
source: Between 700 ms and 2 s following word onset the EEG was comparable between the two conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Starting 50 ms before and ending 260 ms following word onset, frontal and occipital electrodes recorded an amplified voltage for subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords in the Trough condition.
source: Starting 50 ms before and ending 260 ms following word onset, frontal and occipital electrodes recorded an amplified voltage (larger frontal negativity and larger occipital positivity) for subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords in the Trough condition (Figure 3B, frontal cluster: cluster-level Monte Carlo p=0.016 at –50 ms to 260 ms; occipital cluster: cluster-level Monte Carlo p=0.010 at –50 ms to 260 ms).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the Peak condition, there was no significant difference between subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords.
source: In the Peak condition, there was no significant difference between subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 cluster-level Monte Carlo p>0.53).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the EEG analysis shown in a figure supplement.

claim: There was no significant difference between the EC and CC trials in the Peak and the Trough condition.
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the EC and CC trials in the Peak (cluster-level Monte Carlo p=0.54) and the Trough condition (cluster-level Monte Carlo p>0.37).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the EEG analysis.

claim: The difference map between topographies for subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords in the Trough condition resembled the voltage distribution of a frontal slow-wave trough.
source: The difference map between topographies for subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords in the Trough condition resembled the voltage distribution of a frontal slow-wave trough (see Figure 3C, voltage distribution of a prototypical trough).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sleep-learning in the Trough condition benefited from a pronounced trough during stimulus onset.
source: Hence, sleep-learning in the Trough condition benefited from a pronounced trough during stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EEG findings.

claim: Prototypicality differentiated significantly between correctly (higher prototypicality) versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords at 36 hr.
source: Prototypicality differentiated significantly between correctly (higher prototypicality) versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords at 36 hr (p=0.005, FDR corrected: q Benjamini-Hochberg = 0.0125; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The comparison of prototypicality remained significant when comparing the area under the prototypicality curve (AUC).
source: This comparison remained significant when we compared the area under the prototypicality curve (AUC; p<0.019,–150 ms to 350 ms, FDR corrected: q Benjamini-Hochberg = 0. 02).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: The other trough aspects (GFP, ITC, time difference) did not differentiate significantly between subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords.
source: The other trough aspects did not differentiate significantly between subsequently correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords (all p>0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: Trough-targeted word pairs versus pseudowords enhanced the theta power at 500 ms following word onset.
source: Trough-targeted word pairs versus pseudowords enhanced the theta power at 500 ms following word onset (0.2 s to 0.7 s, cluster-level Monte Carlo p=0.018, no significant cluster for Peak-targeted word pairs, p>0.1, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Trough-targeted word pairs versus pseudowords enhanced the fast spindle power at 1 s following word onset.
source: Trough-targeted word pairs versus pseudowords enhanced the fast spindle power at 1 s following word onset (0.8 s-1.2 s, cluster-level Monte Carlo p=0.012, no significant cluster for Peak-targeted word pairs, p>0.4, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The average theta enhancement in the significant cluster correlated significantly with retrieval performance.
source: The average theta enhancement in the significant cluster correlated significantly with retrieval performance (theta: R=0.57, p=0.027, Figure 5A), while the spindle enhancement did not correlate with retrieval performance (spindle: R=0.034, p=0.9, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The spindle enhancement did not correlate with retrieval performance.
source: The average theta enhancement in the significant cluster correlated significantly with retrieval performance (theta: R=0.57, p=0.027, Figure 5A), while the spindle enhancement did not correlate with retrieval performance (spindle: R=0.034, p=0.9, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The comparison between correctly and incorrectly assigned pseudowords did not yield any significant cluster in the theta- or spindle-band power following word onset.
source: The comparison between correctly and incorrectly assigned pseudowords did not yield any significant cluster in the theta- or spindle-band power following word onset (window: 0–2.5 s, cluster-level Monte Carlo pTheta >0.6; pSpindle >0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spectral analysis.

claim: Measures of neural complexity provide non-linear estimates of the variability and 'randomness' of the EEG signal and indicate the amount of information available in the signal at each channel.
source: Measures of neural complexity provide non-linear estimates of the variability and 'randomness' of the EEG signal and indicate the amount of information available in the signal at each channel.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of neural complexity measures based on established knowledge.

claim: Neural complexity is indicative of both the brain's capacity to process sensory information and the extent of ongoing cognitive activity.
source: Neural complexity is indicative of both the brain's capacity to process sensory information (Waschke et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2019) and the extent of ongoing cognitive activity (Höhn et al., 2023; Parbat and Chakraborty, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Levels of neural complexity closely correspond to the depth of sleep.
source: Furthermore, levels of neural complexity closely correspond to the depth of sleep (Casali et al., 2013; Höhn et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2018; Türker et al., 2023), with the lowest levels typically observed during SWS.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Periods of elevated neural complexity are associated with a heightened propensity to process verbal information during sleep.
source: Within sleep, periods of elevated neural complexity are associated with a heightened propensity to process verbal information.
evidence: This is a statement based on previous research findings.

claim: Andrillon and Kouider, 2016 reported larger lateralized readiness potentials indicating correct semantic categorization of words during sleep when words were played during states of elevated neural complexity.
source: Andrillon and Kouider, 2016 reported larger lateralized readiness potentials indicating correct semantic categorization of words during sleep when words were played during states of elevated neural complexity.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

source: Finally, sleep-learning may allow for the reactivation and the subsequent modification and reframing of unwanted memories without the need to consciously re-experience the stressful memories (He et al., 2015; Taschereau-Dumouchel et al., 2018a; Taschereau-Dumouchel et al., 2018b; Zhu et al., 2022).

claim: Thirty participants were included in the final analyses, whereof 15 were assigned to the Trough condition and 15 to the Peak condition.

evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: All included participants were right-handed and reported normal hearing abilities and the absence of mental and physical illness.

claim: The 30 participants slept for a mean of 59.3 min (SEM 24.11 min) before the experimenter woke them.
source: The 30 participants slept for a mean of 59.3 min (SEM 24.11 min) before the experimenter woke them.

source: They spent a mean of 32.3 min in slow-wave sleep (SEM 12.70 min).

claim: Total sleep time did not differ between the Peak-targeted and the Trough-targeted participant sample.
source: Total sleep time did not differ between the Peak-targeted and the Trough-targeted participant sample (Peak: MPeak = 67.4 min, SEM = 27.2 min; Trough: MTrough = 51.1 min, SEM = 18.0 min, t=–1.929, p>0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing sleep duration between conditions.

claim: The duration of slow-wave sleep was significantly shorter for the Trough-targeted participant sample than for the Peak-targeted participant sample.
source: The duration of slow-wave sleep was significantly shorter for the Trough-targeted participant sample than for the Peak-targeted participant sample (Trough: MSWS = 26.3 min, SEMSWS = 15.7, Peak: MSWS = 38.2 min, SEMSWS = 14.0; t=–2.9, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing slow-wave sleep duration between conditions.

claim: The inter-trial stimulus interval (ISI) was shorter in the Trough than the Peak condition.
source: Furthermore, the inter-trial stimulus interval (ISI) happened to be shorter in the Trough than the Peak condition (Peak: MISI = 6.3 s, SDISI = 2.6 s; Trough: MISI = 3.3 s, SDISI = 1.1 s; p<0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing ISI between conditions.

claim: Neither the length of the ISI nor the duration spent in slow-wave sleep correlated with retrieval accuracy at 36 hr.
source: Importantly, neither the length of the ISI nor the duration spent in slow-wave sleep (both z-transformed; N=30) correlated with retrieval accuracy at 36 hr (ISI: r=–0.017, p=0.93; slow-wave sleep duration: r=–0.11, p=0.56).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analyses.

claim: The length of the ISI and the duration spent in slow-wave sleep do probably not account for the difference in retrieval performance between the Trough and the Peak condition.
source: Therefore, the length of the ISI and the duration spent in slow-wave sleep do probably not account for the difference in retrieval performance between the Trough and the Peak condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation results.

claim: The number of words played during slow-wave sleep did not differ between the Peak and the Trough condition.
source: Of note, the number of words played during slow-wave sleep did not differ between the Peak and the Trough condition (Peak: MPeak = 24.2, SD = 3.6; Trough: MTrough = 24.1, SD = 4.3; p>0.95).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing the number of stimuli between conditions.
